title: Two Fatal Shootings Expose Deep Flaws in ICE's Rapid Hiring and Officer Vetting
excerpt: An AP investigation finds recruits with bankruptcies, misconduct histories, and incomplete background checks deployed to the streets, as two people not targeted by warrants are killed in separate incidents within a week.
body:
• ICE is hiring 12,000 new officers to double its force, but an AP investigation found recruits with bankruptcies, prior misconduct lawsuits, and incomplete police academy records.
  • Two fatal shootings in July — in Houston and Biddeford, Maine — killed individuals who were not the targets of ICE operations, and neither incident produced body camera footage.
  • Current officers say new recruits are being deployed before completing mandatory background checks or receiving security clearances.
  • DHS Secretary Mullin briefly paused ICE traffic stops after the shootings, but President Trump reversed the decision within 24 hours.

A Hiring Spree Under Scrutiny

When ICE received a $75 billion congressional windfall to execute the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, the agency launched an unprecedented recruitment drive — 12,000 new officers and special agents to double its enforcement force. More than 220,000 applications poured in. Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons told Congress in February he was proud of the effort, calling it "a well-trained and well-vetted workforce."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=j_Nu0aUqekA

The evidence tells a different story. An Associated Press investigation examining more than 40 new hires who publicized their ICE positions on LinkedIn found several with histories of unpaid debts leading to legal action, two who had filed for bankruptcy, and three who faced lawsuits alleging misconduct in prior law enforcement roles.

"If vetting is not done well and it's done too quickly, you have higher risk of increased liability to the agency because of bad actions, abuse of power and the lack of ability to properly carry out the mission because people don't know what they are doing."

— Claire Trickler-McNulty, former ICE official under three administrations

One recruit, Carmine Gurliacci, had filed for bankruptcy twice and cycled through six Georgia law enforcement agencies in three years before joining ICE. Another, Andrew Penland, left his Kansas deputy position after a $75,000 settlement over allegations he arrested a woman on false charges. A third, Antonio Barrett, initially failed to graduate from a police academy and lasted just three weeks in his only local policing job.

Deadly Consequences in the Field

The vetting concerns have taken on lethal urgency. On July 7 in Houston, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop. Less than a week later, on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during an attempted vehicle stop. Neither man was the target of the enforcement operation. Neither shooting produced body camera footage, despite Congress appropriating $20 million for ICE body cameras earlier this year.

In Biddeford, doorbell camera footage captured six gunshots. A neighbor, Daniel Boucher, told reporters he watched from his window as agents pulled a bleeding man from a white Kia. "He was talking. He said, 'I tried to stop,'" Boucher recounted. Immigrant advocacy groups confirmed Durán Guerrero was a Colombian national with a work permit and Social Security number, a delivery driver with a wife and three-year-old daughter.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin initially told Maine Senator Angus King that the man killed had "weaponized the vehicle," then called back hours later to correct himself — the man was not the operation's target. "The person they were after was not the guy they ended up shooting," King told CNN.

Overworked, Undertrained, and Breaking Down

Current ICE officers speaking to the Washington Examiner painted a picture of an agency buckling under political pressure. One officer said leadership was pushing to "get new recruits guns and badges quick," while veterans described new hires deployed to the streets before completing mandatory federal background checks or receiving security clearances.

"We're being pushed to a breaking point. I don't know where it will go, but it's nowhere good."

— Current ICE officer, speaking anonymously

The workload compounds the problem. Officers report canceled leave, mandatory overtime, and no days off for weeks. "No one is happy," one officer said, directly contradicting former border czar Tom Homan's public claims about agency morale. A former ICE academy instructor, Ryan Schwank, testified before Congress that the agency had cut training on use of force, firearms safety, and the rights of protesters.

Former FBI supervisory agent James Hamilton noted that federal agents are poorly suited to traffic stops — the very tactic now at the center of the deadly encounters. "Federal agents are not good at car stops. Nothing has changed since the '80s," he said, noting he made roughly 3,000 traffic stops as a sheriff's deputy but only one as a federal agent.

Policy Whiplash on Traffic Stops

The back-to-back fatalities triggered a rare internal reckoning. DHS Secretary Mullin ordered ICE to suspend most vehicle stops nationwide, pending additional training. President Trump reversed the pause within 24 hours, posting on social media that stops would continue. ICE officers told the Washington Examiner the agency has no approved traffic stop or vehicle pursuit policy.

Meanwhile, accountability infrastructure is shrinking. The FBI will no longer investigate confrontations involving ICE and other federal officers. In 2025, the Justice Department shut down the National Law Enforcement Accountability Database, which contained disciplinary records for more than 4,000 officers — nearly a quarter from Customs and Border Protection.

What It Means for Immigrant Communities

The enforcement surge extends well beyond those named on ICE warrants. Federal agents arrested 10,000 people in just five days at the end of June. In Memphis, nearly half of ICE arrests since January involved people with no criminal convictions. About 80% of those arrests began with traffic stops — the same tactic that produced the two fatal shootings.

For immigrant communities across the country — including Indian Americans in mixed-status families or those navigating the immigration system — the pattern raises fundamental questions about the balance between enforcement and safety. When officers without completed background checks conduct operations that kill people who are not even their targets, the gap between enforcement and accountability becomes impossible to ignore.
